title: Taking the Whole Clan? How a Tanzania Family Safari Works With Zanzibar at the End
meta_title: Tanzania Family Safari for Groups, With Zanzibar
meta_description: Plan a Tanzania family safari for several families: vehicles, rooms, children's park fees, malaria advice and a 9-day route ending on Zanzibar.
excerpt: How to plan a Tanzania family safari for a group of families or three generations, from vehicles and family rooms to children's park fees and Zanzibar beach days.
content:
A Tanzania family safari for a group of families or three generations works best as a private trip of 8 to 10 days: a gentle start in Tarangire, a crater day in the Ngorongoro, two or three nights in the Serengeti, then a few lazy days on a Zanzibar beach to finish.

The hard part for the organiser is not the wildlife but fitting a grandparent who dislikes bumpy roads, a teenager who wants lions and a four-year-old who naps at noon into the same itinerary. This guide sets out how we plan vehicles, rooms, ages, fees and health for these groups. For how we run trips for several families together, see our family group safari planning page.

Quick Facts

  • Ideal length: 8 to 10 nights: 5 or 6 on safari, 3 or 4 on Zanzibar
  • Classic route: Arusha, Tarangire, Ngorongoro Crater, central Serengeti, Zanzibar
  • Vehicles: One Land Cruiser per six travellers so every child has a window
  • Children's park fees: Free under 5; reduced rates from 5 to 15 (checked November 2026)
  • Malaria: Risk in all areas below 1,800 metres, including the Serengeti and Zanzibar (CDC)
  • Entry extras: Tanzania eVisa plus mandatory inbound travel insurance of US$44 per visitor since 1 October 2026
  • Group bookings: Each family can pay separately; one written quote for the whole party

How Does a Tanzania Family Safari Work for a Group?

A Tanzania family safari for a group is a private, tailor-made trip: your families share guides, vehicles and the same lodges, but each family keeps its own room and can pay its own share. Nobody joins from outside your party, so the pace follows your children rather than strangers.

That matters more than it sounds on a Tanzania family safari. On a shared group tour, the couple who want to stay at a lion sighting for an hour will win over your restless six-year-old every time. On a private trip, the guide can turn back for lunch, stop for a toilet break at a picnic site or swap a long afternoon drive for the pool. Private trips also let grandparents choose an easier vehicle seat and the front row for the shorter drives.

Vehicles and seating for a Tanzania family safari

Northern Tanzania safaris run in 4x4 Land Cruisers with pop-up roofs. Most seat six or seven, but we plan for six so that children are never stuck in a middle seat. When a party is larger, families with similar ages share a vehicle, and the vehicles meet for lunch and at the lodge.

Group sizeVehiclesHow we usually split it
4 to 6 travellers1 Land CruiserOne extended family together, grandparents in the front rows
7 to 12 travellers2 Land CruisersSplit by family or by children's ages, swapping on some days
13 to 18 travellers3 Land CruisersTeens in one vehicle, young children with parents in the others
19 or more4+ Land CruisersTwo lodges of the same standard may be needed on busy dates

Rooms that work for families

Family rooms and interconnecting rooms are the first thing to sell out on any Tanzania family safari. Many lodges in Tarangire, Karatu and the central Serengeti have a few family units, so a group of three or four families should book 9 to 12 months ahead for July, August or December. Where family rooms run out, two adjoining tents with a parent in each is a safe, common solution.

Which Ages Suit Which Safari Activities in Tanzania?

Children of all ages can join game drives in Tanzania's parks, as there is no national minimum age for a drive. The limits come from lodges and activity operators, who set their own rules for walks, balloon flights and shared vehicles, so check every activity in writing before you book.

Here is how age usually shapes a Tanzania family safari for a multi-generation group. Treat it as a guide, because each lodge's policy is what counts:

  • Under 5: Free park entry, short drives of two to three hours, lodges with fenced pools, and a private vehicle so you can head back when they tire.
  • 5 to 11: The sweet spot for a first safari. Children this age love spotting animals and handle half-day drives with snacks and a picnic.
  • 12 to 15: Ready for full-day drives in the Serengeti, cultural visits and longer evening talks with the guide. Some lodges allow guided bush walks from about this age.
  • 16 and over: Pay adult park fees and can join most activities, including walking safaris where they are offered.
  • Grandparents: Ask for the smoothest seats near the front, ground-floor rooms and a rest afternoon after the crater day.

Hot air balloon flights over the Serengeti carry minimum ages and sometimes height rules set by each operator, so confirm before you promise one to a child. Teenagers and adults can fly while younger children enjoy a lie-in at camp. Our guide to planning a safe family safari with children covers bush safety rules, such as staying with an adult after dark.

A 9-Day Route From Tarangire to the Zanzibar Coast

The best route for a Tanzania family safari on the northern circuit starts close to Arusha and builds up to the Serengeti, so the first days have short drives. Three beach nights at the end give everyone time to rest before the long flight home.

DayWhereWhy it works for families
1Arrive at Kilimanjaro Airport, transfer to Arusha (about 1 hour)Short first day; pool and early night
2Tarangire National ParkAbout two hours' drive; elephants and baobabs ease everyone in
3Karatu or the crater rimAfternoon at the lodge, a farm or a village visit
4Ngorongoro CraterHalf-day or full-day crater drive, then back to the lodge
5 to 6Central SerengetiTwo full days of game drives with a midday rest at camp
7 to 9ZanzibarFly about 2 hours from the Serengeti to the coast; beach, snorkelling and Stone Town

If your group prefers fewer road days, a Tanzania family safari can fly into the Serengeti instead. Our 8-day family Tanzania and Zanzibar safari flies about an hour from Arusha to Seronera, spends three nights at Serengeti Serena and finishes with three beach nights. For milestone birthdays and reunions, the 9-day Tanzania celebration safari adds bush dinners and a dhow cruise to the same parks.

When to travel

Most groups plan a Tanzania family safari around school holidays: July and August are dry and busy, with the migration in the northern Serengeti, while late December to February brings the calving herds to the southern plains. Easter falls in the long rains, when some camps close, so ask before fixing dates. Our month-by-month guide to the best time to visit Tanzania has the detail by park.

Why the Ngorongoro Crater Is the Best Big Day for Children

The Ngorongoro Crater is the easiest place in Tanzania for children to see a lot of wildlife quickly. The crater floor holds lions, elephants, buffalo, hippos, zebras and wildebeest, plus a chance of black rhino, within a few hours' drive, and there are picnic sites with toilets.

The crater rim sits well above 2,000 metres, so mornings are cold. Pack fleeces and hats for everyone, especially for children sitting under an open roof. Families with young children often do a half day in the crater and spend the afternoon at the lodge, while older children usually manage a full day.

The crater fee is charged per vehicle, which makes this the best-value day of a Tanzania family safari. Six people in one Land Cruiser share a single fee. Read our guide to Ngorongoro Crater lodges to compare staying on the rim with staying in Karatu, which is usually cheaper and closer to good family rooms.

Adding Zanzibar Beach Days to the Safari

Zanzibar is the natural end to a Tanzania family safari: a short scheduled flight from Arusha or the Serengeti airstrips, warm sea, and hotels with family rooms and calm beaches. Three or four nights is enough for the children to swim, the adults to rest and everyone to see Stone Town.

Where you stay on the island matters for children on a Tanzania family safari. Beaches on the east coast have big tides that leave the sea far out at low water, which is great for rock pools but not for swimming at all hours, while the north has deeper water closer to shore. A dhow sunset cruise, a spice farm visit and a half day in Stone Town suit most ages. Our guide to adding Zanzibar to a safari compares the beaches.

How Much Does a Tanzania Family Safari Cost for a Group?

A Tanzania family safari costs from about US$4,120 per adult and US$2,060 per child for our 8-day family trip with flights to the Serengeti and Zanzibar. Final prices depend on dates, lodge level, children's ages and how many share each vehicle and room.

Group pricing for a Tanzania family safari follows a simple logic. Vehicle, guide and crater fees are fixed costs per vehicle, so they fall per person as each vehicle fills. Park fees are charged per person per 24 hours, and children pay far less. Rooms are the variable that moves most: a family of four in one family room costs less than two double rooms.

Park fees for adults and children

These are the main entry fees for non-resident visitors, including VAT, checked in November 2026. Confirm with Tanzania National Parks before you travel, as fees change.

ParkAdult (16+), per 24 hoursChild (5 to 15), per 24 hours
Serengeti National ParkAbout US$83 in peak seasonAbout US$24
Ngorongoro Conservation AreaAbout US$71, plus US$295 crater fee per vehicleAbout US$24
Tarangire and Lake ManyaraUS$59 in high seasonAbout US$18
Children under 5FreeFree

Two other costs catch out families planning a Tanzania family safari. Most foreign visitors to mainland Tanzania now need the government's inbound travel insurance, US$44 per visitor and valid up to 92 days (checked November 2026), even if you already have your own policy; travellers from East African and SADC countries may be exempt, so check with the insurer. Each traveller also needs a visa; our Tanzania visa guide explains the eVisa, and our full guide to Tanzania park fees covers concession fees inside the Serengeti.

Health, Documents and Safety for Children

Children on a Tanzania family safari need malaria advice, up-to-date routine vaccines, their own passport and, if arriving from a yellow fever country, a vaccination certificate. See a travel clinic six to eight weeks before departure.

Malaria and vaccines

The CDC's Tanzania travel health page lists malaria risk in all areas below 1,800 metres, which covers Tarangire, the Serengeti and Zanzibar; the Ngorongoro rim sits higher, but you pass through risk areas on the way. Children need tablets dosed by weight, plus repellent, long sleeves at dusk and nets. The CDC also advises that all travellers, children included, be fully vaccinated against measles before travel.

Yellow fever and arrival rules

Tanzania asks for a yellow fever certificate from travellers aged one year and over who arrive from a country with yellow fever risk, including after a long transit there (CDC, checked November 2026). Families flying via Nairobi from Kenya should read our yellow fever requirements for Kenya and Tanzania before booking flights.

Safety on the trip

Lodges in the parks are unfenced, so on a Tanzania family safari children are escorted to and from their rooms after dark and must stay inside the vehicle on drives. We suggest each family carries copies of passports and children's birth certificates, plus a written consent letter if a parent is not travelling, since airlines and border officers can ask for proof of guardianship.

Insider Tips

  • Name one organiser: One person collects ages, rooming and dietary needs, so the quote is right first time
  • Plan for six per vehicle: A window for every child stops arguments and keeps the photos coming
  • Book family rooms first: Lodges hold only a few; secure them before flights for July, August and December
  • Build in a rest afternoon: After the crater day, a pool afternoon keeps everyone happy
  • Pack layers: Crater mornings are cold; Zanzibar afternoons are hot
  • Buy the insurance early: Purchase Tanzania's inbound cover online before you fly to save time at arrivals

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a Tanzania family safari suitable for young children?

A Tanzania family safari suits children of most ages if the route is planned around them. Under-fives enter the parks free, but long drives tire toddlers, so keep drives short, add pool time and use a private vehicle. Camp age rules vary, so check each lodge in writing first.

How many people fit in one safari vehicle in Tanzania?

Most safari Land Cruisers used in northern Tanzania seat six or seven passengers, but a Tanzania family safari works best with no more than six in each, so every child gets a window and a pop-up roof view. A group of ten to twelve usually travels in two vehicles, with families or similar ages sharing.

Do children pay park fees in Tanzania?

Children aged 5 to 15 pay reduced park fees in Tanzania, about US$18 a day in Tarangire and Lake Manyara and about US$24 in the Serengeti and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, while children under five enter free (checked November 2026). The Ngorongoro crater fee of US$295 is charged per vehicle, so a full family vehicle shares it.

Do we need malaria tablets for a Tanzania family safari?

Yes, most families need malaria tablets for a Tanzania family safari. The CDC lists malaria risk in all areas of Tanzania below 1,800 metres, which includes Tarangire, the Serengeti and Zanzibar. A travel clinic will choose the right tablet and dose for each child by weight and age, so book an appointment six to eight weeks before you fly.

Can several families share one Tanzania safari and pay separately?

Several families can share one Tanzania family safari and still pay separately. We quote the whole group, then split the total by family, with each family paying its own deposit and balance. On our group safari packages, every seventh place is free when six travellers pay, and people can arrive on different flights and join in Arusha.

Final Thoughts

A Tanzania family safari for a group comes together when you plan around the youngest and oldest travellers: short early drives, six to a vehicle, family rooms booked early and a beach finish on Zanzibar. Get the fees, malaria tablets and insurance sorted in good time, and the wildlife does the rest.
